findings.headline: Adult Social Care faces £1.8m of identified risks from market cost pressures and provider fee demands
findings.detail: While currently forecasting a balanced position, ASC has identified £1.8m of risks from increasingly complex care needs, hospital discharge activity, rising demand, and providers seeking higher fees for high-dependency placements. Market capacity constraints are reducing provider availability.
findings.matters: Care market inflation is national but uncontrolled at local level. Provider fee pressure will escalate as more councils enter deficit positions in this area.
findings.figures: £1.8m identified risks, additional £1m reserve funding for Beachcroft Care Home remedial works
findings.quote: providers seeking higher fees for high-dependency placements and wider market challenges resulting from limited provider capacity

findings.headline: Cavendish Car Park disposal yields £25m capital receipt but erases £1.976m annual rental income, now funded from reserves
findings.detail: Sale completed July 2026 after buyer exercised option early. While the one-off capital receipt of £25m plus £17m deferred benefit supports capital programme, the loss of recurring rental income must be offset from reserves annually, reducing future budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Trading capital assets for one-off liquidity, while accepting permanent income loss, indicates balance sheet strain and reliance on asset sales.
findings.figures: £25m immediate receipt, £17m deferred, £1.976m annual rental income loss
findings.quote: The loss of annual investment rental income for Corporate Property (£1.976m). The loss of rental income is being funded from reserves.

findings.headline: Reserve drawdown strategy: £9.840m drawn from general fund balances plus £38.025m from earmarked reserves to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council is explicitly relying on reserve depletion to balance the budget. Drawdowns include £6.4m from Temporary Accommodation reserve (as transitional support), £7.263m from Property Reserve (including £1.976m to offset rental income lost after Cavendish Car Park disposal), and £2.5m from Service Design reserve.
findings.matters: Structural budget gaps are being masked by reserve usage. This is not sustainable and signals underlying revenue pressures remain unresolved.
findings.figures: £9.840m general fund balances, £38.025m total earmarked drawdowns, forecast reserves £199.386m by year-end
findings.quote: An equivalent sum of £9.840m is budgeted to come from general fund balances.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant moving into deficit in 2026/27, with 14 of 34 schools (41.2%) in licensed deficit
findings.detail: Westminster schools face falling pupil numbers (primary surplus capacity 22.9% as of October 2025, up from 18.9% in May), while high needs expenditure drives DSG into deficit. Fourteen schools hold revenue balance deficits of 7%+ (well above the 10% threshold triggering DfE action plans). Only six have agreed recovery plans; four schools are unable to produce plans.
findings.matters: School deficits are a future budget liability. The high proportion in deficit signals system-wide financial stress, not isolated issues. DfE oversight imminent.
findings.figures: 14 of 34 schools in deficit (41.2%), 6 with agreed recovery plans, 4 unable to produce plans, £2.254m high needs overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: The DSG is expected to move into an overall deficit in 2026/27 as a result of high needs expenditure.

findings.headline: Business Rates collection rate fell 2.07% year-on-year to 33.63% due to legislative changes and billing delays
findings.detail: Q1 business rates collection at 33.63% (vs 35.70% prior year) reflects disruption from the 2026/27 Business Rates Reset and significant legislative changes to multipliers and relief schemes effective 1 April 2026. Billing delays followed, with collection rates expected to take time to stabilise.
findings.matters: Collection delays create cash flow uncertainty. Cyber incident compounded the problem, and council cannot forecast when rates will stabilise.
findings.figures: 33.63% collection rate vs 35.70% prior year, 2.07% shortfall
findings.quote: As of June 2026 the business rates collection rate to date is 33.63%, which is 2.07% lower than the same month last year. This reflects the impact of the 2026/27 Business Rates Reset and the implementation of significant legislative changes to the business rates multipliers and relief schemes from 1 April 2026. These reforms have increased the complexity of the annual billing process and have resulted in delays in billing at the start of the financial year.

findings.headline: HRA in deficit at Q1 with depleted reserves now at £11.631m and requiring £2.194m drawdown by year-end
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account reports £875k deficit at quarter 1. After drawing £2.118m from reserves in 2025/26 for corporate recharges and regulatory costs, HRA reserves fell to £11.631m. The HRA must now generate £2.194m surplus to return reserves to target of approximately £14m.
findings.matters: HRA is a ringfenced account. Depleted reserves and running deficits indicate structural funding gap that cannot be cross-subsidised from General Fund.
findings.figures: £875k Q1 deficit, £11.631m reserves (down from target ~£14m), £2.194m recovery needed by year-end
findings.quote: An overall surplus of £2.194m is required by the end of the year to return reserve balances to the previously anticipated target level. This follows a £2.118m draw on reserves in 2025/26 to manage pressures arising from corporate recharges, depreciation, and the significant impact of new legislative and regulatory requirements.

findings.headline: Cyber incident left cash balances one-third lower, reducing investment income by £2m
findings.detail: Average cash balances have fallen from £739m to £495m year-on-year, a £244m reduction. This reflects cash flow forecasting disruption following the recent cyber incident and unwinding of payment backlogs. The reduced balances force the council to hold more cash in low-yield liquid investments, compounding the income loss.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents affecting core treasury operations indicate a governance and resilience weakness. The income loss is permanent while cash recovers.
findings.figures: £495m current vs £739m prior year (down £244m, ~33%), £2m investment income shortfall
findings.quote: Average cash balances year to date have been approximately £495m, compared with £739m over the equivalent period last year, a reduction of around one-third.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand still rising despite £10m efficiency programme, at 4,540 households
findings.detail: TA placements have surged 67% since 2022, reaching 4,514 households by end-March 2026 and 4,540 by end-June. Despite a dedicated transformation programme extracting £10m in savings, demand continues to grow. The council is relying on this programme's success to contain future costs, with £6.4m drawn from reserves in 2026/27 as transitional support.
findings.matters: This is a structural housing demand crisis on top of HRA finances. If the transformation programme stalls, the council faces an open-ended funding liability.
findings.figures: 4,540 households (67% increase since 2022), £10m annual saving achieved, £6.4m reserve drawdown in 2026/27
findings.quote: TA placement numbers have surged by 67% since 2022, with TA household numbers reaching 4,514 at the end of March 2026. As of 30 June 2026, 4,540 households were living in temporary accommodation, an increase of 26 from the 2025/26 year-end position.

findings.headline: Looked After Children placements escalating in cost, with 27 now exceeding £200k annually, up from 23 last year
findings.detail: Children's Services reports a £5.656m overspend, primarily from Family Services placements. While the total number of looked-after children remains stable at 205, the complexity and cost of placements have increased significantly. Four placements now exceed £500k per year, compared to two in the prior year.
findings.matters: This is uncontrolled, demand-driven cost inflation that cannot be easily managed. The trajectory shows worsening complexity, not abatement.
findings.figures: 27 placements >£200k (prior year: 23), 4 placements >£500k (prior year: 2), total LAC £3.700m overspend
findings.quote: While the total number of LAC are stable with 205 children currently looked after, there have been increases in the number of these that are higher cost and the prices of these more complex placements have increased. There are currently 27 placements costing in excess of £200k per year, with 4 of these costing more than £500k. At the end of 2025/26, there were 23 active placements costing in excess of £200k per year and 2 of these costing more than £500k.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Q1 projected year-end overspend of £7.256m driven by Children's placements and reduced income
findings.detail: The Q1 General Fund is showing a variance of £6.803m, with £3.737m of potential pressures and £3.284m of opportunities identified, giving a current projected variance (overspend) at year-end of £7.256m. The variance mainly comes from higher-cost Children's Services placements and reduced treasury and property income. However, 97.84% of the 2026/27 savings requirement (£45.560m of £46.567m) is either achieved or currently on track, indicating that the core savings programme is largely holding.
findings.matters: A projected year-end overspend signals that emerging pressures (particularly in placements) are outpacing in-year savings delivery, indicating potential draw on reserves if not reversed.
findings.figures: £6.803m variance at Q1; £3.737m pressures; £3.284m opportunities; £7.256m projected year-end overspend; £46.567m savings requirement with £45.560m achieved or on track (97.84%)
findings.quote: The Q1 General Fund is currently showing an £6.803m variance, with £3.737m of potential pressures and £3.284m of opportunities identified. This gives a current projected variance (overspend) of £7.256m at year-end. The variance mainly comes from higher-cost Children's Services placements and reduced treasury/property income

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Capital housing schemes delayed by Building Safety Regulator resource constraints; Gateway 2 applications taking 40+ weeks
findings.detail: Building Safety Regulator resource constraints are creating significant delays in Gateway approvals for higher-risk buildings. Some Gateway 2 applications are taking in excess of 40 weeks, and the regulator is requesting extensions of time in many cases. This poses a significant programme risk for schemes including Ebury Phase 2 (currently progressing through Gateway 2) and 291 Harrow Road (will require Gateway approval in due course). If schemes are delayed, there would be reputational damage, time and cost impact, and delays to start and completion. Church Street Site A has received Gateway 2 approval; approval for Ebury Phase 2 is still pending.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage affects both the council's housing objectives and the financial return assumptions underpinning these regeneration schemes. A lender would track whether delays compress future cashflows or increase borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Gateway 2 applications taking in excess of 40 weeks; Church Street Site A Block A2 secured Gateway 2 approval; Ebury Phase 2 approval still pending; 291 Harrow Road will require future Gateway approval
findings.quote: We have been informed that some Gateway 2 applications are taking in excess of 40 weeks with the regulator requesting extensions of time in many cases. Indication is that resource challenges at the Building Safety Regulator are a key reason for the delays. If schemes are delayed, there would be reputational damage, time and cost impact, and delays to the start and completion of schemes. The risk remains active until all approvals are received

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Awaab's Law Phase 2 implementation deadline 30 November 2026; significant compliance risk identified
findings.detail: Awaab's Law Phase 2 comes into force on 30 November 2026 and significantly expands the range of housing hazards subject to legally enforceable investigation and remediation timescales. In addition to damp and mould, the legislation applies to excess cold and heat, fire and electrical risks, structural safety, falls and hygiene concerns. The council identifies a material risk that it is unable to consistently identify, assess, track and resolve qualifying hazards within the required statutory timescales, heightened by the need for coordinated working across multiple services and contractors.
findings.matters: A finance director would track whether resource and system readiness exist to meet the statutory deadline without triggering breach notices. A lender would assess reputational and financial exposure if the council fails compliance.
findings.figures: Deadline 30 November 2026; substantial increase in volume of repairs covered by legal timeframes; dedicated Awaab's Law readiness programme in place
findings.quote: Awaab's Law Phase 2 is due to come into force on 30 November 2026 and will significantly expand the range of housing hazards subject to legally enforceable investigation and remediation timescales... The risk is that the Council is unable to consistently identify, assess, track and resolve qualifying hazards within the required statutory timescales

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman Tier 1 enforcement notification issued; action plan due 7 October 2026
findings.detail: Westminster has received a Tier 1 Paragraph 49 Notification from the Housing Ombudsman, requiring assurance that the council understands identified issues and plans are in place for sustained service improvements. The Ombudsman found the council's maladministration rate (though improved from 79% in 2023/24 to 55% in 2025/26) is a statistical outlier compared with other landlords, with upheld complaints and compensation levels also identified as outliers. Recurring themes identified include complaint handling, communication with residents, record-keeping and compensation application. A comprehensive response and action plan must be submitted by 7 October 2026.
findings.matters: An Ombudsman enforcement action indicates governance control weaknesses in a material landlord function affecting resident satisfaction and legal compliance. Both lender and finance director would monitor whether remedial action halts the outlier position.
findings.figures: Maladministration rate reduced from 79% (2023/24) to 55% (2025/26); 20 cases reviewed showed recurring themes; cyber incident delayed improvements between November 2025 and mid-February 2026
findings.quote: Westminster City Council has received a Tier 1 Paragraph 49 Notification from the Housing Ombudsman. This represents the earliest stage of the Ombudsman's Further Investigations Framework... the volume of upheld complaints and the level of compensation awarded were identified as statistical outliers when compared with other landlords... A comprehensive response and action plan must be submitted to the Housing Ombudsman by 7 October 2026

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Children's high-cost placements escalating: 20 children costing £7.4m annually (51% of all placement spend)
findings.detail: The council faces sharply escalating costs for children in care with complex behavioural and mental health needs. Twenty children are forecast to exceed £200,000 annually in placement costs, with the highest single placement at £865,530 per year. The combined annual cost for these 20 placements is £7,413,851—an additional £1m more than the total costs of the 22 highest cost placements in 2025/26. This represents a 51% share of total placement spend for over 500 looked after children and care leavers.
findings.matters: A finance director tracking control of statutory service costs would see this as uncontrolled demand and price escalation in a core budget area. A lender would flag the absence of a demonstrated capacity constraint or hard ceiling on these costs.
findings.figures: Highest weekly placement cost £18,698; 20 children forecast to exceed £200,000 annually; highest annual cost £865,530; total for 20 highest-cost placements £7,413,851; increase of £1m from prior year 22 highest-cost placements; 51% of £145.6m total placement spend
findings.quote: the highest weekly placement cost is currently £18,698, and there are 20 children whose placements are forecast to exceed £200,000 annually. The highest forecasted annual cost for this year is £865,530... Of the 20 children whose placement costs are forecast to exceed £200,000 the year, the total annual cost is forecast at £7,413,851. This is an additional £1million more than the total costs of the 22 highest cost placements in 2025/26. This year's forecast represents 51% of total placement spend

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Audit and Performance Committee Performance Report
findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £161m by 2030-31 with £106m savings requirement over three years
findings.detail: The Council's medium-term financial position shows a gap rising from £71m in 2027-28 to £161m by 2030-31. Government grant funding is expected to reduce by £75m by 2028-29, potentially rising to £100m from 2029-30 if transitional protection ends. Around £106m of planned savings are required over the next three years to close this gap, with Fit for the Future expected to deliver at least £30m recurring savings by 2028-29.
findings.matters: A lender would assess whether the council's transformation programme can reliably deliver the savings required to maintain service delivery and financial stability through the forecast period.
findings.figures: £161m gap by 2030-31; £71m gap in 2027-28; £75m funding reduction by 2028-29; £106m savings required over 3 years; Fit for Future targeting £30m recurring savings
findings.quote: the updated MTFP identifies a gap of £71m in 2027-28, rising to £161m by 2030/31. Delivery of significant recurring savings – around £106m of planned savings are required over the next three years

findings.headline: Council signalling that current medium-term oversight of material receipt assumptions may be insufficient
findings.detail: Finance team notes 'the current in year quarterly monitoring reports are focused on in year activity as opposed to impacts over the medium term' and recommends 'separate reporting for capital receipts across the different categories with the opportunity to raise where receipt timing or values have been updated and the impacts of those changes on the financing of the programme'. Committee asked to 'Consider the necessity for separate annual reporting'.
findings.matters: Finance team flagging that governance framework may lack adequate visibility of medium-term receipt and borrowing trajectory; material assumptions lack sufficient medium-term oversight
findings.figures: £881.4m receipts over 15 years; current quarterly monitoring in-year only, not medium-term
findings.quote: However, the current in year quarterly monitoring reports are focused on in year activity as opposed to impacts over the medium term. It may be necessary to instead have separate reporting for capital receipts across the different categories

findings.headline: Largest receipt source (£360m repayments) is contingent on delivery of development schemes
findings.detail: Repayments from Westminster Builds, council entities and Joint Venture partnerships (Ebury Bridge, Church Street JV) total £360.4m – 41% of all receipt assumptions. These are noted as 'Dependent on the delivery of the underlying schemes and the timing of planned repayments'. If schemes pause, change scope, or encounter delivery problems, these repayments won't materialize.
findings.matters: Largest single receipt category is contingent on successful delivery of complex regeneration schemes; any scheme pause or scope change eliminates this funding source without fallback
findings.figures: £360.359m repayment of investment in council entities and joint ventures (41% of £881.392m total)
findings.quote: Dependent on the delivery of the underlying schemes and the timing of planned repayments

findings.headline: Receipt shortfalls would increase borrowing on MTFP already strained by government grant reductions
findings.detail: Council explicitly notes that 'Slippage, reduction or non-delivery of receipts would increase the Council's borrowing requirement, increase capital financing costs and place additional pressure on the Medium-Term Financial Plan which is already challenging given loss of government grant through the fair funding review.' The net borrowing requirement of £1.274bn assumes receipt delivery.
findings.matters: Council faces dual squeeze: reduced government funding AND material delivery risk on £881m of receipts; any shortfall requires additional borrowing or expenditure cuts, worsening revenue budget pressure
findings.figures: £881.4m receipts assumed; £1.274bn net borrowing requirement; £2.549bn capital programme
findings.quote: Slippage, reduction or non-delivery of receipts would increase the Council's borrowing requirement, increase capital financing costs and place additional pressure on the Medium-Term Financial Plan which is already challenging given loss of government grant through the fair funding review

findings.headline: Three-quarters of assumed capital receipts deferred to 2029/30 onwards, creating timing and affordability risk
findings.detail: Of £881.4m total receipts assumed over 15 years, only £31.6m is forecast in 2025/26–2028/29. The remaining £850m is concentrated in 2029/30 and later years: £242.6m in 2029/30, £187.5m in 2030/31, and £419.6m in 2031/32–2039/40. Any delay in scheme delivery or property sales would require temporary borrowing and increase interest costs.
findings.matters: Significant timing risk on a material component of capital programme funding; delays create medium-term cash flow pressure and higher financing costs on an already constrained MTFP
findings.quote: The majority of the forecast capital receipts are expected in 2029/30 onwards as shown in the table below

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account drawing on reserves due to building safety and regulatory costs
findings.detail: The HRA reported a draw on general reserves in 2025/26 largely due to increased regulatory requirements including building safety and fire safety measures (including costs on Lisson Green estate and Awaabs Law compliance). Internal overheads recharged from General Fund also exceeded budget, mainly insurance and digital investment.
findings.matters: HRA reserve depletion signals the council faces unexpected unfunded costs from building regulation changes. These are unlikely to diminish and will require either rent increases or General Fund support.
findings.figures: HRA reserves drawn down in 2025/26; no specific figure given
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account has reported a draw on its general reserves in 2025/26, largely due to the need to respond to an increase in regulatory requirements, including building safety and fire safety measures, such as those on the Lisson Green estate and Awaabs Law.

findings.headline: Schools sector in deficit with 14 schools in deficit and £4.4m cumulative shortfall
findings.detail: 14 schools ended 2025/26 in deficit with overall deficits increasing by £184k to £4.369m (after write-off of £1.073m for five amalgamated schools). DSG cumulative surplus down to just £1.259m, with no headroom against continuing EHCP pressures. EHCP numbers grew 6% year-on-year versus forecast 3%.
findings.matters: School deficits are recurring and councils have limited ability to force school closure. As DSG surplus depletes, council will face pressure to subsidise school deficits from General Fund.
findings.figures: 14 schools in deficit; deficits increased £184k to £4.369m; DSG surplus £1.259m; EHCP growth 6% vs 3% forecast
findings.quote: 14 schools ended the year in deficit, with overall deficits increasing by £0.184m to £4.369m (after the amalgamation of five schools into two with the write off of £1.073m for those school's deficits) and overall net school balances (including surplus balances) of £2.503m.

findings.headline: Council tax increase of up to 100% of council element under discussion
findings.detail: The government has removed council tax referendum limits for six authorities, including Westminster. A 100% increase in Westminster's council element (£537/year) would add £83m to council income but still leave Westminster below council tax levels in Camden (£2,207) and Brent (£2,235). No council tax increase is yet reflected in the budget gap forecast.
findings.matters: A 100% increase in council tax is politically extreme and there is no certainty this will be accepted by residents. The council is signalling it will engage residents but has not committed to any specific rise.
findings.figures: Current Westminster element: £537/year; potential additional: £83m if doubled; total band D would reach ~£1,610
findings.quote: If Westminster were to raise its element of council tax by 100%, this would be another £537 per year (around £10.33 per week per household). The total Band D council tax would then be around £1,610 a year (assuming the GLA put their element up by 5%). So, an overall increase of 54%. This would generate additional income for the Council of £83m.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising £3.5m per annum with £2.5bn gross capital programme
findings.detail: The council has a £2.5bn gross capital programme (£1.3bn net) over 15 years including a significant housing development programme. Capital financing costs require an additional £3.5m per annum budget provision across all 15 years. Given falling revenue funding, the council notes capital spending will need review "as part of the medium-term financial planning process."
findings.matters: A large capital programme funded by borrowing against a shrinking revenue base creates ongoing financial burden. Review of capital spending is being flagged, suggesting capital schemes may be deferred or cancelled.
findings.figures: £2.5bn gross capital spend; £1.3bn net; £3.5m per annum financing requirement
findings.quote: The current MTFP includes additional budget provision of £3.5m per annum to finance the cost of the capital programme. This additional annual budget provision will be required across the fifteen years of the capital programme to finance the expenditure plans that are currently in the Capital Strategy.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand and cost pressures requiring £6m additional provision over MTFP
findings.detail: Adult Social Care faces sustained demand-led pressures driven by care package increases, placements and hospital discharges. The council has added £4.3m in 2026/27 and a further £3m in both 2027/28 and 2028/29 to the MTFP. Care providers are seeking higher contract uplifts due to London Living Wage and non-pay cost increases, creating ongoing price pressure.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led and cost-driven by factors beyond the council's control (LLW, care complexity). The paper signals this will continue, not stabilise.
findings.figures: £4.3m additional in 2026/27; £3m further in both 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: Adult Social Care continues to face growing demand and cost pressures, driven by increases in care packages, placements and hospital discharges. These pressures are expected to continue into 2026/27. An additional £4.3m has been included in the 2026/27 budget, with a further £3m built into the MTFP in both 2027/28 and 2028/29

findings.headline: Children's social care overspending with ongoing complexity and £3.3m recurring pressure
findings.detail: Children's Services had a £6.3m overspend in 2025/26, with £3.3m relating to ongoing increased complexity of need. High-cost placements are expected to continue into 2026/27, leading the council to allocate additional budget of £3.3m in 2027/28. This indicates the overspend is structural, not one-off.
findings.matters: Recurring overspends in children's social care indicate the council is unable to control costs in a statutory service. The complexity is rising, not falling, suggesting pressures will continue or worsen.
findings.figures: £6.3m overspend in 2025/26; £3.3m recurring complexity element; £3.3m additional budget allocated 2027/28
findings.quote: The Children's Services outturn position for 25/26 was a £6.3m overspend against budget. Of that amount, £3.3m related to ongoing increased complexity of need within children's family services Those high-cost placements are expected to continue into 2026/27

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation placements up 67% to 4,514 households with no sustainable reduction plan
findings.detail: Westminster has seen a 67% increase in TA placements since 2022, reaching 4,514 households at end of 2025/26. The paper identifies this as "the most significant pressure on the Council's finances over the last four years." The council has allocated £5m one-off funding plus £550k for specialist resources in 2026/27, but the paper shows this as a cost pressure, not a solution plan with measurable reduction targets.
findings.matters: TA is a demand-led, open-ended cost driven by high London rents and welfare policy. At current growth rates, this will consume an increasing share of the budget and is difficult for the council to control.
findings.figures: 67% increase since 2022; 4,514 households as of end 2025/26
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation has been the most significant pressure on the Council's finances over the last four years. Westminster has seen a 67% increase in placements since 2022, with TA household numbers reaching 4,514 at the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves drawn down to £51.5m after £8.2m 2025/26 overspend
findings.detail: The General Fund outturn for 2025/26 was an overspend of £8.2m, funded from reserves. This reduces General Fund balances from £59.6m to £51.5m. The paper states reserves "is not a sustainable way of balancing the budget on an ongoing basis" but the council is already using this approach.
findings.matters: Reserves are being drawn to cover recurring service overspends rather than one-off pressures, and at current depletion rate of £8m+ per year, the council faces exhaustion within 6-7 years if the structural deficit is not closed.
findings.figures: £8.2m overspend in 2025/26; reserves fall from £59.6m to £51.5m (18.2% of 2026/27 budget)
findings.quote: This will reduce balances from £59.6m to £51.5m (or 18.2% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget). Adult Social Care continues to face growing demand and cost pressures... These pressures are expected to continue into 2026/27.

findings.headline: Savings plan of £30m falls £76m short of £106m need
findings.detail: The council needs to achieve £106m in savings over three years to balance the budget, but the transformation programme (Fit for the Future) only commits to a minimum of £30m by end of 2028/29. The gap between need and planned delivery is £76m, leaving a £46m shortfall unaddressed even if the £30m is delivered on time. The paper acknowledges "the challenge is set to get much harder."
findings.matters: A savings plan that covers only 28% of the identified need suggests either the budget gap will not close or further announcements of major service cuts are pending.
findings.figures: £106m needed; £30m planned; £76m gap
findings.quote: However, the challenge is set to get much harder with planned savings totalling £106m that need to be achieved over the next three years and more needed to balance the increased budget gap.

findings.headline: £100m annual government grant loss with transitional protection ending
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review will reduce Westminster's grant funding by £75m by 2028/29 with transitional protection phasing the impact. A further £25m of transitional protection grant is assumed to fall out in 2029/30, amounting to a permanent £100m annual loss. This is the primary driver of the budget gap.
findings.matters: This revenue loss is permanent and beyond the council's control, leaving only council tax increases or service cuts as options. The loss is equivalent to 34% of current net revenue budget.
findings.figures: £100m permanent annual loss from 2029/30; £75m loss phased to 2028/29; £25m transitional protection
findings.quote: After the third year of the settlement the level of transitional protection grant being provided as part of Westminster's settlement is £25m. It is expected that this protection will fall out after the third year in 2029/30 thereby amounting to an annual reduction of £100m at that point.

findings.headline: Budget deficit of £161m over four years with no balanced plan
findings.detail: The council faces a total budget gap of £161m to 2030/31, an increase of £73m from the March 2026 forecast. The largest single-year gap is £71m in 2027/28. The paper describes this as "the most significant financial challenge that Westminster City Council has ever faced." The council has not yet identified how to close this gap.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this magnitude with no concrete closure plan signals severe financial stress and suggests either major service cuts, massive council tax rises, or both.
findings.figures: £161m total gap to 2030/31; £71m in 2027/28; £73.4m increase from March forecast
findings.quote: The revised position, over the four years of the new administration, provides an indicative budget gap of £71m in 2027/28, rising to £161m by 2030/31. This is an increased gap of £73m from the previously reported position in March

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: External audit fees overspend by £0.3m
findings.detail: Finance reported an overspend of £0.135m relating to external audit fees which were £0.300m above budget. Partially offset by £0.158m in Redmond Review Audit grant.
findings.matters: A lender should note audit fee escalation as a running-cost pressure on councils.
findings.figures: £0.300m overspend on audit fees; £0.158m Redmond Review Audit grant received
findings.quote: Finance have reported an overspend of £0.135m relating to external audit fees for the financial year 2025/26 which is £0.300m above budget.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Pay award exceeded budget by £0.9m across the council
findings.detail: Corporate Items include a £0.9m overspend from a pay award that was higher than originally budgeted. This is in addition to specific service pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether pay inflation is baked into future budget assumptions or whether this signals further pressure ahead.
findings.figures: £0.9m pay inflation overspend
findings.quote: There is a £2.9m overspend on items held corporately. This includes a £0.9m overspend on pay inflation following a higher pay award than originally budgeted

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Corporate Property cost shock of £3.0m from head lease rent review, empty investment property costs, and prior year business rates
findings.detail: Corporate Property overspent by £1.7m against budget, driven by £3.0m in cost increases. These relate largely to a head lease rent review, empty investment property carrying costs, and prior year business rates and service charges. Partially offset by £1.4m in additional income from rent reviews including backdated rent.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is facing rising occupancy costs or one-off catch-up on prior-year liabilities.
findings.figures: £1.688m overall overspend; £3.045m cost increases; £1.357m additional income from rent reviews
findings.quote: There have been significant cost increases of £3.045m relating largely to a head lease rent review, empty investment property costs and prior year business rates and service charges.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA overspend of £2.1m will require draw from reserves, to be recovered by March 2027
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account was budgeted to break even but ran £2.1m in deficit, driven by £2.9m in additional staffing due to regulatory requirements (building and fire safety, Awaabs Law compliance). This was partially offset by £2.4m savings in repairs and maintenance. The council will draw from HRA reserves to cover the deficit, with a commitment to return balances to planned levels within 12 months.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether HRA reserves are being drawn to cover recurring costs or one-off items, and whether recovery plans are realistic.
findings.figures: £2.1m HRA overspend; £2.9m staffing overspend from regulatory pressures; £2.4m repairs and maintenance savings; recovery plan by March 2027
findings.quote: The overall overspend will require a draw from HRA reserves - however, this sum will be added to the HRA efficiency programme with a view to returning balances to the previously anticipated level by March 2027.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements overspend by £5.5m, with £3.3m driven by increased complexity of need
findings.detail: Children's Services overall overspent by £6.3m (11.8% of budget). The largest pressure is placements at £5.5m, with £3.3m from increased case complexity and £2.2m from prior year disputed costs. Additional pressures from contract inflation above the 3% assumption (£0.7m), legal costs (£0.7m), and transport (£0.4m). Some offset by underspends in registrars (£1.2m from price increases and higher volumes) and education (£1.0m from SEN transport savings).
findings.matters: A lender needs to distinguish between one-off cost pressures and structural caseload growth. Rising complexity suggests growing need, not temporary spike.
findings.figures: £6.336m total Children's Services overspend; £5.5m on placements; £3.3m from increased complexity; £2.2m from prior year disputed costs; £0.7m excess contract inflation; £0.7m legal costs
findings.quote: The most significant pressure relates to Children's Social Care placements (£5.5m), reflecting increased complexity of need (£3.3m), alongside ongoing pressures from prior year disputed costs (£2.2m).

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Cyber incident disrupted TA improvement strategy for 3 months, delaying property purchases and slowing delivery of cost-reduction measures
findings.detail: Loss of key IT systems for 3 months delayed property purchase completions for new lower-cost TA supply and hindered the council's case management and social housing allocation. The incident constrained the council's ability to manage demand and costs during a period of peak pressure. The council allocated £1m from corporate risk reserves in February 2026 to respond; £545k was spent in 2025/26, mostly on staffing and specialist suppliers.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's disaster recovery is adequate for critical systems. Three months downtime on housing systems during a budget crisis is material.
findings.figures: £1m allocated from reserves in February 2026; £545k spent in 2025/26; systems down for 3 months
findings.quote: Loss of key IT systems for 3 months delayed property purchase completions and slowed new lower cost TA supply coming on stream; it hindered the Council's ability to prevent homelessness and secure affordable placements (as case management systems were down) and slowed the allocation of social housing voids.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn and Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £15.8m driven by structural demand and expensive nightly lettings beyond housing allowance limits
findings.detail: TA placements have grown 67% since 2022, reaching a record 4,514 households (4,700 TA units under management) at year end. The council is heavily reliant on expensive nightly-paid accommodation where rents exceed Local Housing Allowance limits. The council has allocated £5m one-off plus £550k recurring in 2026/27 to address this through expanded affordable supply and improved move-on. Demand growth is slowing (homelessness applications down 24% year-on-year), suggesting the worst may be passing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this £15.8m is a one-year spike or a structural hole in the budget. The scale and growth trajectory matter for repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £15.786m overspend; 4,514 TA households at 31 March 2026 (up 321 from 4,193); 67% growth since 2022; 24% drop in homelessness applications year-on-year
findings.quote: TA placements have surged by 67% since 2022, with TA household numbers reaching 4,514 at 31 March 2026 (up 321 from 4,193 last year). This record caseload – equivalent to around 4,700 TA units under management, carries major financial, operational and compliance obligations for the Council.

findings.headline: FOI performance collapsed from 87% to 68% due to cyber incident; Q4 fell to 48%
findings.detail: FOI demand increased to 3,014 requests (from 2,596 prior year). Case management system offline during Q3/Q4 severely degraded response performance. January performance hit only 20% on-time responses; improved to 60% by March. Governance transparency weakened during incident period.
findings.matters: FOI performance is a governance metric watched by lenders and auditors. Degradation to 48% in Q4 and large backlogs suggest potential transparency and accountability weaknesses during a critical period.
findings.figures: 87% to 68% annual performance decline; Q4 48%; January 20%, March 60%
findings.quote: FOI demand increased significantly in 2025/26, with 3,014 requests received compared with 2,596 in 2024/25... overall performance against the statutory response deadline fell to 68% at year end from 87% in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Climate net-zero risk escalated to 25/25 (maximum) at year-end; emissions trajectory significantly off-track
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CR1 (net-zero) rated highest severity. Council emissions are 31% higher than straight-line trajectory to 2030 target. Citywide emissions 40% above modelled trajectory. Risk level explicitly increased at Q4.
findings.matters: Net-zero compliance is increasingly a credit metric for local authorities. Escalating risk designation signals the council may miss statutory targets, with potential regulatory intervention and reputational consequences.
findings.figures: CR1 risk 25/25; council emissions 31% above target trajectory; citywide emissions 40% above target; 29,251 tCO2e vs 19k target
findings.quote: Risk level increased to 25/25 at Q4.

findings.headline: Cyber incident recovery ongoing with 98% of systems restored but operational impacts persisting
findings.detail: Over 400 council digital systems impacted; 98% now restored. Residual impacts include backlogs in housing, complaints handling, FOI responses, and TA delivery delays. Systems used for payments, rent collection, repairs logging and case management were offline during peak quarter.
findings.matters: While recovery is progressing, operational delays in revenue-critical services (rent collection, repairs, homelessness prevention) reduce management visibility and control. Delayed TA acquisitions and prevention activities compounded existing overspend.
findings.figures: 400 digital systems; 98% restored; Q3/Q4 disruption
findings.quote: Of around 400 digital systems in use across the Council, over 98% are now back up and running. Work is continuing with suppliers to restore access to the remaining systems.

findings.headline: Housing rent arrears spiked to £7.9m due to cyber incident disrupting direct-debit collections
findings.detail: Cyber incident prevented rent collection through Direct Debit during disruption. HRA rent arrears reached £7.9m as of 5 April 2026, plus £6m in service charge arrears. Recovery plan in place for 2026/27 but impact on HRA sustainability flagged.
findings.matters: HRA is typically ring-fenced and relied upon for housing delivery programmes. Material arrears reduce liquidity and may constrain capital investment in affordable housing.
findings.figures: £7.9m rent arrears; £6m service charge arrears; total £13.9m housing arrears
findings.quote: The disruption also meant the service was unable to take rent and service charge payments through direct debit with increased arrears across rent (£3.5m) and service charge (£6m).

findings.headline: SEND budget overspend of £601k with flat-cash settlement for 2026/27 increases risk
findings.detail: SEND specialist provision exceeded budget by £601k in 2025/26. Underlying cost drivers remain. Flat-cash budget allocation for 2026/27 reduces capacity to address root causes and creates risk of a second consecutive in-year overspend as demand continues to grow.
findings.matters: A spending pressure that cannot be solved within the current envelope and is expected to recur compounds the general financial sustainability question, especially as demand-led.
findings.figures: £601k overspend 2025/26; flat-cash budget 2026/27
findings.quote: The cost of meeting demand for SEN specialist provision exceeded our budget for 25/26 resulting in an end of year overspend of £601k. We received a flat‑cash budget for High Needs in 2026/27 which reduces our capacity to tackle the root causes and presents a new risk that continuing growth in demand will create a second consecutive in‑year pressure.

findings.headline: Children's placements: 22 children costing £6.8m annually (35% of placement budget)
findings.detail: One child's annual placement cost reached £541,308. Of 500+ looked-after children and care leavers, 22 placements exceed £200k annually, totalling £6.822m. Volatility described as significant due to complex behavioural and mental health needs and ICB restrictive funding interpretation.
findings.matters: A small cohort driving over one-third of placement spend creates budget volatility and dependence on external funding arrangements. Forecast accuracy and demand management are compromised.
findings.figures: £541,308 highest annual placement; £6.822m from 22 placements; 22 placements represent 35% of total spend for 500+ children
findings.quote: Of the 22 children whose placement costs exceed £200,000 per year, the total annual cost was £6,822,408. This represents 35% of total placement spend for over 500 looked after children and care leavers in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £15.9m drives General Fund pressure
findings.detail: TA reported net overspend of £15.916 million at year-end with expenditure of £82.442 million against budget of £64.878 million. 4,514 households in TA as of 31 March, up 321 over the year. Demand growth slowing (first annual reduction in applications since 2021/22) but reliance on high-cost nightly accommodation continues.
findings.matters: A single service line running £16m over budget is a material balance-sheet stress. The council is managing a portfolio comparable to a registered housing provider while facing constrained move-on options and a national housing crisis.
findings.figures: £15.916m net overspend; £82.442m spend vs £64.878m budget; 4,514 households; 321 household increase over year
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation reported a net overspend of £15.916 million at year end, with net expenditure of £82.442 million against a budget of £64.878 million.

findings.headline: Cash reserves declining sharply as council shifts to internal borrowing for capital
findings.detail: Investment balances fell 34% year-on-year from £463.4m to £306.3m. The net cash position deteriorated by £153.3m. The council is explicitly using internal borrowing (drawing down reserves and cash) rather than external borrowing to fund its capital programme, which reduces financial flexibility and working capital buffers.
findings.matters: Falling cash reserves indicate tightening liquidity and reduced capacity to absorb shocks. The shift from having £463m invested to £306m shows the council is consuming cash faster than it generates it.
findings.figures: Investment balances 31 March 2025: £463.4m. 31 March 2026: £306.3m. Decline of £157.1m (34%).
findings.quote: Daily investment balances have steadily decreased from £463.4m at 31 March 2025 to £306.3m at 31 March 2026 which reflects the continued use of internal borrowing to fund the council's capital programme.

findings.headline: Investment income fell 28% short of budget at £11.8m below forecast
findings.detail: The council budgeted £41.5m in investment returns for 2025/26 but achieved only £29.7m. The shortfall is attributed to Bank Rate falling from 4.50% to 3.75% through the year, reducing yields on cash holdings. This is material money the council was counting on to manage its position.
findings.matters: A lender assesses cash generation capacity. A £11.8m miss on budgeted investment income (28% below forecast) affects the council's ability to self-fund operations and reduce reliance on borrowing or reserves.
findings.figures: Budgeted investment return £41.5m, actual £29.7m, variance £11.8m under.
findings.quote: The council's budgeted investment return for 2025/26 was £41.5m, and performance for the year is £29.7m, resulting in £11.8m under budget.

findings.headline: £257m in new lease liabilities added mid-year without prior treasury forecast, pushing gross debt 41% above plan
findings.detail: The council took on £257m in new leases in 2025/26, primarily the A2Dominion transaction which commenced in April 2025 after the Treasury Strategy had been approved in February. This caused gross debt to reach £855m against a forecast of £605m — a £250m increase. The Operational Boundary (a monitoring tool) was exceeded as a result, though the council stayed within its legal Authorised Limit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council can forecast and control its commitments. A £250m gap between forecast and outturn on liabilities suggests either poor planning or a major new obligation approved outside normal treasury processes.
findings.figures: Gross debt forecast £605m, actual £855m. New leases £257m. A2Dominion transaction commenced April 2025.
findings.quote: The Council exceeded the Operational Boundary because the A2Dominion lease transaction commenced in April 2025, after the Treasury Management Strategy and Prudential Indicators had been approved in February 2025. Consequently, the borrowing associated with the transaction was not reflected in the original forecast.

findings.headline: Transformation programme delivering £30m savings is early-stage with only £3m in 2026/27, creating execution risk
findings.detail: A council-wide 'Fit for the Future' transformation programme is forecast to deliver a minimum £30m in savings across the planning period, but only £3m is included in 2026/27 because the programme is still in formative stages with diagnostic work only now being commissioned. Delivery of the full £30m+ is essential to the medium-term financial plan but remains unproven.
findings.matters: The MTFP depends on successful transformation delivery to avoid larger reserve depletion or service cuts. Early-stage programmes carry higher execution risk, especially when the council faces tight timescales and competing pressures.
findings.figures: £30m minimum target; £3m budgeted for 2026/27; £30m represents less than 5% of gross controllable spend
findings.quote: It is estimated that this will deliver a further £30m as a minimum over the planning period. Only £3m is budgeted for in 2026/27 as the programme is in its formative stages, but with a clear approach and structures set up and diagnostic analysis work now being commissioned.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation and adult social care remain volatile high-demand pressures not fully controlled
findings.detail: The report identifies temporary accommodation as a persistent significant cost pressure and adult social care as experiencing rising costs from both increasing demand and complexity of need. While three-year scenario models exist, the council has not yet stabilised these cost drivers and they are forecast to remain pressures.
findings.matters: If these volatile demand-led services overshoot forecasts, the council will be forced to either raid reserves faster, cut other services, or use emergency measures—all signals of financial stress to a lender.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation identified as significant cost pressure requiring three-year scenario planning; Adult Social Care cost rising from demand and complexity
findings.quote: Provision of temporary accommodation for housing has been a significant cost pressure in recent years, so a three-year plan has been produced that models increasing demand and pricing of supply based on different assumptions. Adult Social Care has also seen a rise in costs from increasing demand and complexity of care which is modelled in the MTFP.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs have increased to 5.2% PWLB as favourable forward deals at 2.6% are fully used
findings.detail: Westminster's £400m forward borrowing done in 2022/23 at 2.6% average rate is now fully utilised. All new capital borrowing must be sourced at current PWLB rates of approximately 5.2%, effectively doubling the financing cost of future capital schemes and increasing the annual revenue cost of the capital programme.
findings.matters: Higher capital financing costs reduce the council's ability to fund infrastructure investment and will consume more of the revenue budget, making it harder to balance the General Fund if capital schemes cannot be reduced or delayed.
findings.figures: Forward deals: £400m at 2.6% average; current PWLB long-term rate: ~5.2%
findings.quote: For borrowing purposes, the cost of capital is relatively high with long term rates through PWLB still at around 5.2% and this is now being factored into the medium-term estimates as the previous forward borrowing deals in 2022/23 that obtained £400m of borrowing at an average of 2.6% is now fully utilised.

findings.headline: Reserves being drawn down to balance current budget for the first time, signalling structural stress
findings.detail: Westminster is using £19.7m from reserves in 2026/27 to balance the budget (£9.7m from General Fund, £10m from earmarked), an approach the report describes as unusual for the council. While reserves remain adequate at ~15% of net budget requirement after this draw, the trajectory suggests reserves will be needed again in following years to offset growing gaps.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion for ongoing operations (not one-off costs) is a leading indicator of structural budget stress and limits the council's ability to absorb shocks, fund investments, or smooth volatility in demand-led services.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £54.6m (20% of net budget requirement); £19.7m use in 2026/27; flexible reserves £88m remaining; declining to ~15% General Fund ratio after use
findings.quote: Whilst unusual for Westminster City Council to need to do this and on its own is not a cause for concern, the following two years will require more serious consideration.

findings.headline: Forecast budget gaps of £61m in 2027/28 and £27m in 2028/29 that the CFO says cannot be closed without service reductions
findings.detail: After planned savings of £34m in 2026/27 and before the Transformation Programme is fully delivered, the council faces gaps of £61m then £27m. The Section 151 Officer explicitly states that closing these gaps without significantly affecting services would require raising council tax beyond the normal 5% threshold or finding substantial new income.
findings.matters: The council's own finance officer is signalling that the required budget actions will be material and difficult—either service cuts to significant programmes or politically sensitive council tax rises that may encounter resistance.
findings.figures: £61m gap 2027/28; £27m gap 2028/29; cumulative deficit of £88m annually by year three
findings.quote: it will need to increase its income very significantly or it will need to reduce spending very significantly or a combination of the two to balance its budget.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review creates £100m structural deficit, reducing core grant by 45.9% from £219m
findings.detail: Westminster's government grant allocation is being reduced by £100.4m (45.9%) over three years through the Fair Funding Review redistribution. Even with transitional protection, the council faces a permanent £75.6m annual reduction (34.5%) from 2029/30 onwards. This is a structural shift, not a cyclical pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether a council can absorb a permanent 35% cut to its core grant funding. This fundamentally changes the council's financial model and revenue-raising capacity.
findings.figures: £100.4m total reduction from £219.0m per annum; £75.6m annual reduction by 2029/30 (34.5%)
findings.quote: the target Fair Funding grant allocation for Westminster will reduce by £100.4m from the current £219.0m per annum. This is a reduction of 45.9% in cash terms.

findings.headline: Development scheme delays pose direct revenue risk; 680 new homes' income assumes on-time delivery
findings.detail: The 5-year business plan assumes 680 new homes will be added, generating £2.4m of additional rental income. However, the council explicitly flags the risk: "if schemes experience delays and units are handed over later than profiled which would reduce projected income levels for the HRA in any given year." Major schemes include Ebury phases, Church Street, and others with multi-year construction timescales.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that failure to deliver on capital programmes directly impacts revenue forecasts. Construction delays or cost overruns will reduce projected income.
findings.figures: 680 new homes expected over 5 years; £2.4m of additional income assumed from new development
findings.quote: This assumption also creates a corresponding financial risk for the HRA if schemes experience delays and units are handed over later than profiled which would reduce projected income levels for the HRA in any given year

findings.headline: Repairs budget continues to experience upward pressure despite inflation provisions; planned maintenance inflation risk only tolerated to 3%
findings.detail: Despite allocating inflation provisions, the repairs budget faced upward pressure in 2025/26. The council has assumed 2.6-3.0% general inflation for 2026/27 but the sensitivity analysis shows the plan can only tolerate 3% inflation on Planned Maintenance over the first 3 years before becoming unsustainable. Construction and utilities sectors have experienced "much more severe inflationary pressure."
findings.matters: Upward pressure on costs is already appearing mid-forecast, and the plan has minimal headroom to absorb further inflation. Any inflation above 3% forces borrowing increases or service cuts.
findings.figures: Inflation assumption 2.6-3.0% for 2026/27; £30.1m inflation contingency included in 5-year capital programme; plan failure point >3% on Planned Maintenance over first 3 years
findings.quote: Despite this, the repairs budget has continued to experience upwards pressure in 2025/26, and inflation remains a significant risk in this area. The impact of inflation on the HRA is exacerbated by its exposure to sectors such as construction and utilities which have experienced much more severe inflationary pressure

findings.headline: Pimlico District Heating Undertaking replacement is a £176.8m commitment with no agreed option or fixed costs
findings.detail: The council has committed to replacing PDHU (the district heating network), but no preferred option has been selected. The HRA Business Plan includes estimates ranging across multiple options, all requiring "significant capital investment." Until a preferred option is chosen, the council cannot confirm actual costs or timescale. This is the second-largest single capital category after Major Works.
findings.matters: A lender is committing to finance a major infrastructure project (£176.8m) with unproven costs and delivery timescale. Cost overruns are likely.
findings.figures: PDHU total 30-year investment £176.8m; years 3-5 spend £37m annually; figures in business plan are estimates pending option selection
findings.quote: Until a preferred option for the future provision of heat for customers currently served by PDHU has been selected, the figures included in the HRA Business Plan are estimates but represent a significant proportion of the cost of the options being considered

findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts have collapsed; London discounts dropped from £136,400 to £16,000, eliminating a material funding source
findings.detail: Right to Buy receipts historically provided capital funding. The discount in London has fallen 88% (£136,400 to £16,000), dramatically reducing proceeds. Council projects this will reduce both the number of sales and amount of funding available to support the HRA capital programme.
findings.matters: A funding source that previously supported capital investment is now negligible. This increases reliance on borrowing and other constrained sources.
findings.figures: London Right to Buy discount reduced from £136,400 to £16,000; Right-to-Buy receipts budgeted at only £1.3-10.4m annually
findings.quote: It should be noted that discounts on Right to Buy applications have reduced in London from £136,400 to just £16,000. This is anticipated to reduce the number of homes sold under the Right to Buy scheme, but also reduce the amount of receipts available to fund the HRA Capital Programme

findings.headline: Affordable Housing Fund is already in deficit; council has only budgeted conservatively at £25m over 5 years despite commitments of £41.9m
findings.detail: The AHF currently holds £38.9m but faces commitments of £41.9m, creating an immediate shortfall. The business plan includes only a prudent projection of £25m over the next 5 years. The council acknowledges the risk explicitly: "if these receipts are not received then alternative sources of funding will need to be identified or spending reduced."
findings.matters: A key funding source for housing development is already in deficit. Any shortfall means either borrowed funding or delayed/reduced schemes.
findings.figures: Current AHF forecast balance £38.9m; commitments £41.9m; prudent 5-year projection £25m
findings.quote: The current forecast balance at 31st March 2026 is £38.9m and whilst this is not sufficient to cover commitments that have been made within the existing development programme (which totals £41.9m from 2026/27 onwards), a prudent future projection of £25m over the next 5 years has been built into the revised business, which covers the anticipated draw from this fund, however these are estimates and if these receipts are not received then alternative sources of funding will need to be identified or spending reduced

findings.headline: Rent income is exposed to policy change; the plan fails if government moves from CPI+1% to CPI-only after 2036
findings.detail: The plan assumes rent policy continues at CPI+1% indefinitely. Government has confirmed this for 10 years, but the sensitivity analysis shows the HRA becomes unsustainable if rent policy reverts to CPI only from 2036/37. This gives only a ten-year policy window for what is a 30-year plan. The council has already maximised 2026/27 rent increase at 4.8% and is introducing Rent Convergence, adding £1-2/week from April 2027.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on rent income assumptions that depend on government policy lasting 30 years. Loss of the +1% above inflation after 2036 is a material revenue risk.
findings.figures: Plan failure point: rent increases lower than CPI+1% from 2036/37 onwards; 2026/27 rent increase 4.8% (maximum policy allows)
findings.quote: The HRA BP recognises Governments extension of the existing rent policy to 10 years (assuming the rent uplift ceiling of CPI+1%). The plan can tolerate a CPI only increase from 2036/37 onwards (under a new rent policy)

findings.headline: Interest rates on new borrowing have been raised substantially; plan has only 0.6% headroom to absorb further increases
findings.detail: The council revised its external PWLB borrowing assumption upward to 5.1% for 2026/27 (from previous 3.79-4.0%), dropping to 4.1% from 2029/30. The sensitivity analysis shows the plan can only tolerate an average interest rate of 5.5% on new debt in the first 5 years—just 0.4-0.6% above current assumptions—before it becomes unsustainable. Interest payable grows from £10m to £26m by 2030/31.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know how much interest rate risk the HRA can absorb. This plan has almost none; any further rise will force re-profiling of capital schemes or additional rent increases.
findings.figures: External PWLB borrowing assumed at 5.1% (2026/27), reducing to 4.1%; plan failure point >5.5% average rate; interest payable rises from £9.996m (2026/27) to £25.986m (2030/31)
findings.quote: the Business Plan borrowing rates are assumed to increase to 5.1%, reflecting the anticipated discounted rate of borrowing available to the HRA, reducing to 4.1% over the medium term. In the past the Council has benefitted from a forward borrowing facility that has kept this interest costs relatively low

findings.headline: HRA reserves fall below the minimum 10% threshold in 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The general reserve is projected to fall to 9% of turnover in the first two years of the business plan, below the council's own minimum target of 10%. The council acknowledges this explicitly: "As a result of the additional income being used to meet pressures, rather than contributing to reserves in the short term, the balance on the HRA reserve falls to 9% of turnover in 2026/27 and 2027/28." Reserve balance only grows from £13.7m to £14.7m.
findings.matters: Reserves below target indicate reduced financial resilience and limited ability to absorb unforeseen pressures during the critical period when new borrowing ramps up.
findings.figures: Opening reserve £13.7m; proposed 2026/27 reserve £14.7m (9% of turnover); target minimum 10%
findings.quote: the balance on the HRA reserve falls to 9% of turnover in 2026/27 and 2027/28, before returning to being above the recommended 10% in 2028/29

findings.headline: HRA borrowing is at the absolute limit of what the revenue budget can sustain
findings.detail: The council must borrow an additional £860.3m over 15 years to deliver its capital ambitions, pushing total HRA debt to peak at £1.19bn by 2038/39. The business plan explicitly states this borrowing sits "right at the limit" of what the interest cover ratio of 1.20 can support. The margin between the revised debt profile and the borrowing cap in Chart 1 shows virtually no additional borrowing capacity beyond the plan.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether an authority can service debt. Westminster's HRA has used up all prudent headroom and is vulnerable to interest rate or income shocks.
findings.figures: £860.3m additional borrowing required over next 15 years; debt peaks at £1.19bn by 2038/39; opening debt balance £386.4m
findings.quote: the HRA Business Plan is effectively at the limit of its borrowing capacity overall (see Chart 1 above) in terms of being able to cover the cost of interest within its revenue budget

findings.headline: Pension Fund approves £50m loan to LLP for acquisition and lease-back of council temporary accommodation properties
findings.detail: In November 2025, the Pension Fund Committee approved a £50m loan investment to a council-owned LLP that will purchase selected council TA properties and lease them back under a credit tenant lease structure. The arrangement generates a capital receipt for the council to fund other capital expenditure and reduce borrowing need, with final portfolio selection due in a Cabinet report by March 2026.
findings.matters: A structural financing arrangement between the council and its pension fund to monetise TA assets, with potential pension fund implications and contingent lease obligations if the council cannot meet lease payments.
findings.figures: £50m loan; portfolio selection by March 2026
findings.quote: On 5 November 2025, the Pension Fund Committee approved a £50m loan investment to a Council-owned LLP, which will purchase selected Council-owned temporary accommodation (TA) properties and lease them back under a credit tenant lease structure previously used by the Council... The arrangement will create a lease payment between the Council and the LLP and generate a capital receipt for the Council, which will help fund future capital expenditure and reduce the need for additional borrowing.

findings.headline: External borrowing required in early 2027; council using sinking fund approach to smooth revenue impacts
findings.detail: Cash projections indicate the council will need to borrow externally again in early 2027 at PWLB rates (gilt yield +0.8%). To manage volatility in capital financing costs across 15 years, the council will 'operate a sinking fund approach whereby funding is drawn down from a capital financing reserve in the earlier years...with contributions being made back into the reserve in the later years'.
findings.matters: Confirms need for external market borrowing and reveals the council is using reserve management to mask year-on-year revenue volatility, which defers but does not eliminate the underlying cost pressure.
findings.figures: External borrowing timing: early 2027; rates: gilt yield +0.8%; total net financial costs over 15 years: £931.961m
findings.quote: Current cashflow projections suggest a need to borrow externally again in early 2027. All new loans are subject to the relevant gilt yield +0.8% (certainty rate).

findings.headline: Affordable Housing Fund scheme cost pressures forced reduction in future-year allocations
findings.detail: In 2025/26, multiple housing schemes experienced unforeseen cost increases requiring additional drawdowns from the Affordable Housing Fund. This 'eased the pressure on HRA borrowing but has meant allocations in future years needed to be reduced', with the council relying on future receipts 'which are not guaranteed' to restore the buffer.
findings.matters: Housing schemes exceeded budgeted costs, depleting a key reserve and shifting the timing of funding availability, indicating either cost planning issues or changed site conditions not anticipated.
findings.figures: £25m projected AHF receipts to 2028/29; specific overspend amounts not disclosed
findings.quote: 2025/26 has been particularly challenging, with some schemes needing to access additional AHF funding due to unforeseen events onsite. This eased the pressure on HRA borrowing but has meant allocations in future years needed to be reduced. The expectation is future years receipts will top the pot back up, but these are not guaranteed.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from housing sales are most volatile and uncertain funding source; programme heavily dependent on market
findings.detail: A 'considerable amount' of programme funding comes from capital receipts expected from private unit sales in housing developments, but these 'could be subject to market volatility and macroeconomic circumstance'. The council acknowledges receipts are 'faraway the most uncertain of all funding sources' and maintains only 'a prudent level' of income in budgets.
findings.matters: Significant programme funding depends on house price movements and developer sales performance, creating execution risk and potential need for programme reductions or additional borrowing if markets weaken.
findings.figures: No specific amount disclosed for receipts exposure
findings.quote: A considerable amount of funding in the capital programme is due from capital receipts. These are expected to be generated from the Council's housing development schemes from the sale of private units. However, the value of the receipts could be subject to market volatility and macroeconomic circumstance could impact on the level of receipts the Council receives. Capital receipts have the potential of being the most volatile of capital funding sources and are faraway the most uncertain of all funding sources.

findings.headline: Capital programme revenue costs growing to £89m annually by 2039/40; Fair Funding Review will constrain capacity
findings.detail: The council's annual capital financing budget is currently £24.2m and will reach approximately £89m by 2039/40. The MTFP includes a £3.5m annual increase plus £2m in 2027/28 and £5.5m in 2028/29 specifically for TA financing. However, the incoming Fair Funding Review 'will have a significant impact on the Council's revenue budget' and 'will put the Council's finances under increasing pressure, with savings and strong financial management needed'.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing borrowing costs coincide with a material cut to government funding, creating a squeeze where fixed capital financing charges will consume an increasing share of a smaller revenue base.
findings.figures: Current: £24.2m; by 2039/40: c.£89m; increases of £3.5m baseline, £2m in 2027/28, £5.5m in 2028/29
findings.quote: The implementation of the Fair Funding Review will have a significant impact on the Council's revenue budget, with further information in the main budget report. However, the significant reduction in funding will put the Council's finances under increasing pressure, with savings and strong financial management needed to manage the medium-term position.

findings.headline: Net zero decarbonisation programme loses all government grant funding, shifting cost to council revenue
findings.detail: In June 2025, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero announced it would not commit further investment into the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme. The council notes this will 'significantly impact the pace of delivery' and require the council to use 'more of its own financial resources' to meet its net zero 2030 and 2040 targets, raising 'value for money concerns' for remaining sites.
findings.matters: A material funding stream for a statutory sustainability programme has disappeared, forcing either reallocation of council resources or scaled-back delivery of environmental commitments.
findings.figures: PSDS grant ended June 2025; remaining retrofit sites have higher carbon cost threshold with value-for-money concerns
findings.quote: The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) announced on 11 June 2025 that it would not commit any further investment into the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS). This decision will significantly impact the pace of delivery of the Council's Carbon Management Programme. The remaining sites to be retrofitted have a higher carbon cost threshold as they are lower energy consuming sites. This raises value for money concerns when developing future work programmes. The reduced grant funding landscape will require the Council to use more of its own financial resources if it is to achieve the Fairer Westminster net zero 2030 and 2040 targets.

findings.headline: £170m additional temporary accommodation investment to address council's most significant financial risk
findings.detail: The council is adding £170m to acquire ~460 properties over three years as part of a strategy to move from 75% private-rented to 25% private-rented TA. The average cost difference is material: £50k annually for private-rented units versus £25k for council-owned units including financing costs. The programme aims to generate £4.5m annual savings.
findings.matters: TA is explicitly identified as the council's most significant financial risk, and this programme directly addresses affordability and budget volatility by converting variable revenue spend into fixed assets.
findings.figures: £170m investment, ~460 properties, £50k vs £25k annual unit costs, £4.5m potential annual savings
findings.quote: TA represents the Council's most significant financial risk. This investment mitigates that risk by converting ongoing revenue expenditure into a capital asset base, improving value for money, and reducing exposure to market volatility.

findings.headline: Children's Services staffing savings of £775k are no longer happening
findings.detail: Line 2.2 originally planned staffing savings of £500k in 2025/26 and £775k in 2026/27 (£1,275k total). The revised schedule now shows only £500k will be achieved in 2025/26, with the full £775k marked unachievable. This represents over 60% of the planned Children's staffing savings failing to materialise.
findings.matters: The failure of 60% of planned staffing savings in a critical service area signals either unforeseen obstacles to restructuring, retention issues making headcount reductions impossible, or that the original target was unrealistic. This suggests significant delivery risk elsewhere in the savings plan and potentially rising staffing costs.
findings.figures: £775k of £1,275k planned Children's staffing savings (2.2) is now unachievable

findings.headline: £1,240k of previously approved savings are now unachievable
findings.detail: The council originally planned £50,725k in savings across all services. Following a February 2026 review, £1,240k of these cannot be delivered at all. Children's services accounts for £880k of this (mainly staffing), Regeneration for £300k, and Corporate Services for £60k. The council has partially offset this by reprrofiling £1,170k of savings into 2027/28, but this leaves a net delivery shortfall of £1,240k from the original plan.
findings.matters: Unachievable savings indicate the council is struggling to deliver its financial plan. If savings cannot be found to replace the £1,240k shortfall, the council faces either a larger deficit, need to draw on reserves, or deliver savings in years already heavily loaded. This directly affects the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £1,240k unachievable (Children's £880k, Regeneration £300k, Corporate Services £60k); original total savings plan £50,725k; revised delivery profile £44,569k in 2025/26-2026/27 vs £47,089k planned
findings.quote: Revised Profiling of Savings 44,569 4,806 110 49,485; Total Revised Savings Requirement 2,520 (1,170) (110) 1,240

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Capital Budget Re-Profiling & Budget Changes
findings.headline: Ebury Bridge Estate Equity Loan leaseholder returns are slower than anticipated, with £3.831m reprofiled to 2027/28 as leaseholders defer to future phases.
